--- title: "Arctic Fowl" subtitle: "`polars` and `duckplyr`" description: "Interpreted Languages can have nice things too!" date: 07-04-2025 categories: [R, R-Package, Developer-Toolkit] citation: url: https://asenetcky.dev/posts/2025-05-20-thinking-in-projects/ draft: true --- ## What a Time to be Alive In an era where AI is the all the rage, some of the most exciting things I have encountered and have been playing around with lately have been remixes on old favorites. I'm talking of course about working with dataframes. One of my favorites lately has been [polars](https://pola.rs/) and everytime I'd use `polars` and then eventually do some work in R using the [tidyverse](https://www.tidyverse.org/), I would really feel some of the niceities in `polars` that were missing in my day-to-day R workflow. This is made all the more apparent to me because I adore working with [dbplyr](https://dbplyr.tidyverse.org/) and its ability to lazily evaluate R code as sql expressions and `collect()` the results into memory at a time of my choosing. `polars` brings similar asbstractions to the table, however, instead of a sql table being the target, dataframes are. It's a genius idea that has really changed how I work and think about data and what I am capable of doing with both resource rich, and starved computers before needing to scale up to other tools and techniques (if I even need to scale up at all). ... Enter [DuckDB](https://duckdb.org/), I've always admired DuckDB from a distance. Dabbling here or there. Some friends and colleagues of mine have thoroughly enjoyed it. I write a bunch of SQL code for work, and for me, it has always felt like that - work. I believe that perhaps this has more to do with the locked down work environment with little to no modern tooling availible to anyone outside of IT (like Data Scientists). However, because of the harsh developer experience when dealing with SQL, I try to do the absolute bare minimum I need to do and bail as fast as possible. So DuckDB just never fell into my lap - until now. [duckplyr](https://www.tidyverse.org/blog/2025/06/duckplyr-1-1-0/) joins the `tidyverse` and now we have a fairly seamless drop-in replacement for `dplyr` that leverages a `DuckDB` backend for everything it can, and falls back to regular `dplyr` automatically when handed something it cannot evaluate. For barely any setup at all - you get many of the same bells and whistles of `polars`, but in quite _literally_ a tidy package. Users get their lazy evaluation, their swapping between immediate and deferred execution. Folks can work with data larger than the memory on their computer. Like `polars` there are awesome functions for reading and writing data files. If you're a tidyverse-native like myself, you can do all this without leaving your comfortzone, and why would you want to be anywhere else? In all seriousness, I think this is such an incredible win, `polars` syntax was already fairly similar to `tidyverse` syntax in many ways. There was some cross-over with SQL verbage as well in the `tidyverse`, and DuckDB is in-memory SQL and more. In theory, I now have the ability to be dropped into basically any team working with dataframes, and can just hit the ground running with _good_ options at my disposal regardless of the language of choice and the least amount of impact from context switching. ## Setup You might mutter under your breath: "sure, that is all great, but setup must be a pain" and I would argue no, or at least, it doesn't have to be. Please refer to the documentation for the respective packages, especially as they revolve over time. However, setup might look something like this for most users. ::: {.cell} ::: :::{.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R With`renv` setup might look something like this in the console: ```r renv::install("duckplyr", "dplyr", "conflicted") ``` and then at the top of our R scripts: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} suppressPackageStartupMessages({ library(conflicted) library(duckplyr) conflict_prefer("filter", "dplyr") |> suppressMessages() }) ``` ::: You _technically_ don't even need `conflicted`, but using that package will provide a smoother user experience, and the explicitness in the will help with reproducibility. ## Python I'm using `uv` for python - so setup in the terminal would look _something_ like this: ```bash $ mkdir my-project-folder $ cd my-project-folder $ uv init $ uv add polars ``` and then at the top of our python scripts (or bottom of your marimo notebooks ;p): ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import polars as pl ``` ::: ::: ## Taking a Look If it wasn't obvious before, I want to say this isn't going to be post where I pick a favorite and sell you on it. I really enjoy both packages and programming languages. At the time of writing this, I am primarily an R programmer. I have spent more time with python polars than anything duckdb-related, and quite a bit of time recently with polars. Still, all of the time with python has been considerably less time compared to R. I have experimented a little bit with the duckdb cli tool in the past, but nothing more than an afternoon or two. This is my first real foray into working with the `duckplyr` package. All this to say, that I am not an expert in either of these tools and I am likely not working with them in the most idiomatic way. I'm mostly just here to crush parquet files and have a good time. `duckplyr` has some example data bundled with the package. We'll work with that. First we'll save to parquet file into a temporary folder. In the real world ::: {.callout-note} Ideally, users would just use the data in memory and pass it around between the languages using something like `arrow` and `reticulate` to handle zero-copy streaming etc... However, I think using local files more clearly displays the pros of these packages - so that is the route we're going to take. ::: ### Example Data ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(fs) my_temp_dir <- fs::file_temp() |> fs::dir_create() data_path <- fs::path(my_temp_dir, "temp-flight-data", ext = "parquet") # save path to python object py_data_path <- reticulate::r_to_py(data_path) duckplyr::flights_df() |> duckplyr::compute_parquet(data_path) |> invisible() ``` ::: These data aren't large by any means, but they are readily available - and `duckplyr` uses these data in their documentation. I was able to use 7GB+ parquet files on my humble laptop working with the same code below without crashing my IDE, which is a modern miracle. ### Nanoparquet I want to take a quick aside and mention that `nanoparquet` has some nice tools for inspecting parquets without reading the entire file into memory as well. [nanoparquet](https://nanoparquet.r-lib.org/) is completely dependency free and a worthy companion to `duckplyr`. Since we have a parquet file - let's take a quick peek, and then go back to using the `duckplyr` and `polars`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(nanoparquet) # grab very basic info about the file and data structure info <- nanoparquet::read_parquet_info(data_path) ``` ::: ```r # grab much more granular information about the data schema schema <- nanoparquet::read_parquet_schema(data_path) # grab the info above and more! metadata <- nanoparquet::read_parquet_metadata(data_path) ``` ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # scope out the basic info glimpse(info) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Rows: 1 Columns: 7 $ file_name "/tmp/RtmpQSJtrs/filed34e22183c2/temp-flight-data.parq… $ num_cols 19 $ num_rows 336776 $ num_row_groups 3 $ file_size 5813818 $ parquet_version 1 $ created_by "DuckDB version v1.3.1 (build 2063dda3e6)" ``` ::: ::: We have the parquet, we know the data's basic dimensions, and we know that the number rows probably won't blow up our IDE session. Let's dive in, but we'll pretend there are a few more 0's after that `info$num_rows` and show off how we might dance around that problem. ## Diving Right In We're going to look at some common actions side by side. :::{.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ducks <- read_parquet_duckdb( data_path, prudence = "stingy" ) # no collect - notice the row count ducks |> head() |> arrange() |> collect() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 6 × 19 year month day dep_time sched_dep_time dep_delay arr_time sched_arr_time 1 2013 1 1 517 515 2 830 819 2 2013 1 1 533 529 4 850 830 3 2013 1 1 542 540 2 923 850 4 2013 1 1 544 545 -1 1004 1022 5 2013 1 1 554 600 -6 812 837 6 2013 1 1 554 558 -4 740 728 # ℹ 11 more variables: arr_delay , carrier , flight , # tailnum , origin , dest , air_time , distance , # hour , minute , time_hour ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} ducks |> head() |> collect() |> glimpse() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Rows: 6 Columns: 19 $ year 2013, 2013, 2013, 2013, 2013, 2013 $ month 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1 $ day 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1 $ dep_time 517, 533, 542, 544, 554, 554 $ sched_dep_time 515, 529, 540, 545, 600, 558 $ dep_delay 2, 4, 2, -1, -6, -4 $ arr_time 830, 850, 923, 1004, 812, 740 $ sched_arr_time 819, 830, 850, 1022, 837, 728 $ arr_delay 11, 20, 33, -18, -25, 12 $ carrier "UA", "UA", "AA", "B6", "DL", "UA" $ flight 1545, 1714, 1141, 725, 461, 1696 $ tailnum "N14228", "N24211", "N619AA", "N804JB", "N668DN", "N394… $ origin "EWR", "LGA", "JFK", "JFK", "LGA", "EWR" $ dest "IAH", "IAH", "MIA", "BQN", "ATL", "ORD" $ air_time 227, 227, 160, 183, 116, 150 $ distance 1400, 1416, 1089, 1576, 762, 719 $ hour 5, 5, 5, 5, 6, 5 $ minute 15, 29, 40, 45, 0, 58 $ time_hour 2013-01-01 10:00:00, 2013-01-01 10:00:00, 2013-01-01 10… ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # basic group by ducks |> # notice the use of `.by` in summarise and not group_by() summarise( count = n(), .by = month ) |> head(n=5) |> arrange(month) |> collect() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 2 month count 1 1 27004 2 2 24951 3 3 28834 4 4 28330 5 5 28796 ``` ::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} bears = pl.scan_parquet(r.py_data_path) # collect into a dataframe bears.head().collect() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ::: ## Taking a step back Killer features: ### Lazy Evaluation `polars` and `duckplyr` are both able to lazily evaluate data transformations. Users can take objects in-memory, or a file, and queue up actions to perform later on. Why is this important? This is primarily a plus when working with large amounts of data that you could not possibly store into the RAM of your computer, or it would be prohibitively expensive to provision a cloud computer with the amount of RAM needed to. What if our example data was a 7GB parquet file and it was 259 million rows long. I couldn't possibly hope to read that whole file in _and then_ start filtering and grouping and other data wrangling. Lazy evaluation allows users to effectively stream the data from memory or a file, taking only the needed bits, doing only the necessary operations, and doing nothing more. Delaying the execution of actions also allows for the packages to implement query optimization, where the user describes the steps and what they want to see and the package will work out the best steps to get there. ### So Fast TODO: duckplyr prudence lavish - "think eager" always materialize stingy - avoid spending at all cost thrifty - use memory wisely polars lazyframe -lazy and dataframe eager.
